title: On 20 October 2010, the San Francisco Metro Transit Authority and the California Public Utilities Co
description:
On 20 October 2010, the San Francisco Metro Transit Authority and the California Public Utilities Commission delivered UberCab a cease-and-desist order. The company was barely four months old; TechCrunch had covered its launch that July.

The taxi industry's complaints were specific: no taxi licence, different insurance than licensed taxis, and pickups without the hour's advance booking the law required for limos. Real regulatory objections, not just a turf war.

potential jail time threatened for each day UberCab kept operating past the order, on top of a $5,000 fee per instance.

The company didn't fight over the name. Within days, UberCab became simply Uber, on its website, its blog, and in a company comment reading "more uber than cab". CEO Ryan Graves told TechCrunch only that the company was working with the agencies to figure out their exact concerns.

Because Uber was brand new, it paid for uber.com in company equity rather than cash: shares in a business barely worth anything yet. Universal Music Group held the domain from an unrelated failed venture, then sold its stake early. Fortune reported in 2014 the missed gain topped $100 million.

Sources:
- https://techcrunch.com/2010/10/24/ubercab-ordered-to-cease-and-desist/: primary reporting from 24 October 2010, confirms the San Francisco Metro Transit Authority and California Public Utilities Commission delivered UberCab a cease-and-desist order on 20 October 2010, the taxi industry's specific complaints (no taxi licence, different insurance, immediate pickups without the hour's advance booking limos required), penalties of up to $5,000 per instance of operation plus up to 90 days' jail per day of continued operation, CEO Ryan Graves' quoted response, and the company's rebrand from UberCab to Uber within days including the "more uber than cab" comment.
- https://fortune.com/2014/06/04/universal-music-group-sold-uber-domain/: primary reporting from 4 June 2014 confirming Universal Music Group acquired Uber shares through its investment in an unrelated, since-shut-down startup also called Uber.com, that Universal sold the domain (and its equity) to the ride-hailing Uber for equity rather than cash around 2010, that Universal cashed out its stake early for what the article calls "a nominal profit", and that Universal would have made more than $100 million had it held on, given Uber's reported $17 billion valuation as of May 2014.
